extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: A dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task, requiring broad discourse context.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.publisher: CIMeC - Center for Mind/Brain Sciences, University of Trento; Institute for Logic, Language & Computation, University of Amsterdam
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The LAMBADA dataset was constructed from the Book Corpus. Passages were filtered using four language models to remove easy cases. Remaining passages were evaluated by human subjects via the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: guessing the target word from the whole passage, verifying with a second subject, and ensuring the word could not be guessed from the target sentence alone by up to 10 subjects. Only passages where two consecutive subjects guessed correctly from the broad context and no subject guessed correctly from the local context were included.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), containing unpublished novels.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list were performed on the Book Corpus. Passages were filtered based on language model probabilities and human evaluation results.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The Book Corpus underwent duplicate removal and filtering of offensive material. Passages were split into training and development+testing partitions. A random sample of passages was subjected to human evaluation to filter for items requiring broad context. The final dataset consists of 10,022 passages.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects were recruited via CrowdFlower. For each passage, subjects guessed the target word from the whole passage. If correct, a second subject verified. Then, up to 10 subjects attempted to guess the word from the target sentence alone. If no subject could guess it, the passage was included. Subjects were paid per page.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The criteria for inclusion were strict: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word, and no subject out of ten could provide it based on local context only. This hit-or-miss approach was chosen over allowing synonymous continuations due to the difficulty and cost of determining substitutability at scale.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Multiple (up to 12 subjects per item in the filtering pipeline: 2 for broad context verification, up to 10 for local context rejection)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN), standard 4-gram model, feed-forward model, and another RNN trained on the Book Corpus were used to filter out easy passages.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The development set and training corpus are available for download. The test set was planned to be made available at the time of a public competition.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text, moving beyond statistical generalizations.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are hugely overrepresented in LAMBADA (48%) compared to the input data, while common nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are under-represented. This bias makes co-reference easier than other discourse phenomena.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging by design, as it filters out passages solvable by local context. Standard language models are bound to fail on it. The strict inclusion criteria (exact match) may exclude passages with plausible synonymous continuations. The dataset is limited to English novels.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of computational models for text understanding, specifically testing the ability to keep track of information in the broader discourse. It serves as a challenging test set for language modeling and natural language understanding research.
